concepts.def: The state in which particles are packed closely in a fixed arrangement, so a solid keeps its own shape and volume.
The state in which particles are still close together but can move past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
The state in which particles are far apart and move randomly, so a gas fills whatever container it is put in.
The one temperature at which a substance melts and at which it also freezes. Solid to liquid and liquid to solid both happen at this temperature.
The one temperature at which a substance boils and at which it also condenses. Liquid to gas and gas to liquid both happen at this temperature.

concepts.term: Simple model of the three states
concepts.def: A model in which the particles of a substance are represented by small solid spheres, arranged closely and regularly in a solid, closely but randomly in a liquid, and far apart in a gas.
The attractions holding the particles of a substance to one another. Their strength depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
The energy that must be supplied to separate particles from one another. The stronger the forces between the particles, the more energy is needed and the higher the melting point and boiling point.
(HT only) In the simple model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are shown as spheres, and the spheres are shown as solid.
A property such as melting point, colour, hardness or electrical conductivity that belongs to a large collection of particles arranged in a structure, not to a single atom.
The letter or letters written in brackets after a formula in a chemical equation to show the state of that substance: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid and (g) for gas.
A solution made by dissolving a substance in water. It is shown in an equation by the state symbol (aq).
The regular structure formed by an ionic compound, in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in a repeating three-dimensional arrangement.
The attraction between oppositely charged ions. In a giant ionic lattice these forces are strong and act in all directions.

concepts.term: High melting and boiling points of ionic compounds
concepts.def: Ionic compounds melt and boil at high temperatures because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds in the lattice.
When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water the ions become free to move, so charge can flow and the substance conducts electricity.
A substance whose particles are small groups of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Such substances are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points.
The weak force of attraction between one molecule and another. It is these forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two atoms inside a molecule.
Molecules are neutral, so a molecular substance has no charged particles that are free to move and it does not conduct electricity.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
A substance whose molecules are very large. The atoms in a polymer molecule are joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, usually forming a long chain.

concepts.term: Why polymers are solids at room temperature
concepts.def: Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
A structure in which all of the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil the substance.
Diamond and graphite, which are forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide, also called silica.
The strong bonding in the giant structure of atoms that makes up a metal. It means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.

concepts.term: Layers of atoms in a pure metal
concepts.def: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers. The layers can slide over one another, which allows metals to be bent and shaped.
A mixture of a metal with other metals. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed to make alloys, which are harder.
Electrons in a metal that are free to move through the whole structure. They carry electrical charge through the metal, so metals conduct electricity well.
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred through the metal by the delocalised electrons.
A substance is solid below its melting point, liquid between its melting point and its boiling point, and gas above its boiling point.

mcqs.q: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?
options: At its melting point, the same value as for melting
At its freezing point, a lower value than melting
At its boiling point, where condensing happens
At any temperature far below room warmth
mcqs.explain: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point.

mcqs.q: Bromine vapour is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which change of state is this, and at which temperature does it happen?
options: Condensing, at the condensing point of bromine
Condensing, at the boiling point of bromine
Freezing, at the melting point of bromine
Condensing, at bromine's melting point
mcqs.explain: Boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.

mcqs.q: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?
options: As spheres drawn to the true size of an atom
As spheres that swell when the solid melts
As small solid spheres of the same kind
As tiny cubes stacked in a neat grid
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in this model particles are represented by small solid spheres.

mcqs.q: A solid is heated until it melts. Using the simple particle model, what happens to the particles?
options: They soften and change into smaller spheres
They break up into several smaller particles
They lose their shape and flow into each other
They stay the same but move further apart
mcqs.explain: A change of state alters the arrangement and movement of the particles, not the particles themselves.

mcqs.q: Substance X melts at 801 degrees C and substance Y melts at -7 degrees C. What does this tell you about the two substances?
options: The particles in X must be much heavier than in Y
The forces between the particles in X are much stronger
Substance Y has no forces between its particles
Y has stronger forces, so it melts much sooner
mcqs.explain: The stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting point.

mcqs.q: Why do some substances need much more energy to boil than others?
options: Because the particles they contain are larger and heavier
Because they have to be heated for a much longer time
Because the forces between their particles are stronger
Because a greater mass of substance is being used
mcqs.explain: The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.

mcqs.q: (HT only) Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the three states of matter?
options: The model draws far too few particles to be realistic
The model cannot explain any melting or boiling at all
The model shows solid, liquid and gas apart
The model shows no forces between the particles
mcqs.explain: The specification lists the absence of forces as one of the limitations of the simple model.

mcqs.q: (HT only) In the simple model the particles are solid inelastic spheres with no forces between them. Why does this make boiling hard to explain?
options: Boiling overcomes forces the model leaves out
The spheres are drawn much larger than real atoms
The model uses far fewer particles than a real sample
The particles in the model move much too slowly
mcqs.explain: Energy is needed at the boiling point to overcome forces between particles, and the model contains no forces.

mcqs.q: Ethanol melts at -114 degrees C and boils at 78 degrees C. What is the state of ethanol at 25 degrees C?
options: Gas, because 25 degrees C is above the melting point
Solid, because 25 degrees C is far below 78 degrees
Liquid, because 25 degrees C lies between the two values
Liquid and gas together in about equal amounts
mcqs.explain: A substance is a liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.

mcqs.q: Substance P has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. What is the state of P at 20 degrees C?
options: Liquid, since 20 degrees C is above its melting point
Solid, because both quoted values are below zero
Liquid, which is normal at room temperature
Gas, since 20 degrees C is above its boiling point
mcqs.explain: Above the boiling point the substance is a gas, whatever sign the quoted values carry.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C but chlorine melts at -101 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?
options: Sodium chloride has strong ionic attractions to break
The covalent bonds inside chlorine break easily as it melts
Chlorine has fewer bonds, so it melts a lot sooner
Sodium chloride particles are much heavier than chlorine
mcqs.explain: Different bonding gives forces of very different strengths, so far more energy is needed to melt the ionic lattice.

mcqs.q: A student says that one copper atom is shiny, can be bent and conducts electricity. Why is this wrong?
options: A single atom is shiny but it cannot conduct
Bulk properties belong to whole structures
Only atoms that are inside a compound gain them
An atom is too small to see, so nothing is known
mcqs.explain: Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity come from very many atoms arranged and bonded together.

mcqs.q: What does the state symbol (aq) tell you about a substance in an equation?
options: It is a liquid, whether or not it is water
It is the water used as the solvent here
It is a gas bubbled through the mixture
It is dissolved in water to give a solution
mcqs.explain: (aq) shows an aqueous solution, that is a substance dissolved in water.

mcqs.q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
options: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(l) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)
mcqs.explain: The metal is solid, the acid and the salt are dissolved in water, and hydrogen is given off as a gas.

mcqs.q: Calcium carbonate chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?
options: CaCO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(l) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
mcqs.explain: The chips are solid, the acid and the salt are aqueous, the water is a pure liquid and carbon dioxide is a gas.

mcqs.q: Why is sodium chloride described as a giant ionic lattice?
options: It is built from millions of NaCl molecules joined up
Every sodium ion is attracted to just one chloride ion
Very many ions sit in a regular repeating pattern
The electrostatic forces act along the rows of ions
mcqs.explain: An ionic compound has a regular structure in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in all directions.

mcqs.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and boiling points?
options: Breaking the many strong bonds needs large amounts of energy
The ions are heavy and packed so tightly they cannot move
Every ion in the lattice repels the ions beside it
The ions must be split into atoms before it can melt
mcqs.explain: This is the reason given by the specification for the high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds.

mcqs.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?
options: Melting releases electrons that can move through the liquid
In the liquid the ions are free to move and carry charge
Melting turns the neutral particles into charged ions
Liquids conduct just like water does, but solids never can
mcqs.explain: When melted, the ions are no longer held in fixed positions, so charge can flow.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride is dissolved in water. Why does the solution conduct electricity?
options: Water itself is a very good conductor of electricity
Dissolving splits the molecules into atoms
The ions separate and are free to move about
The water supplies free electrons to the mixture
mcqs.explain: Dissolving frees the ions from the lattice so that charge can flow.

mcqs.q: Why are substances made of small molecules usually gases or liquids at room temperature?
options: Their covalent bonds are weak and break very easily
Their molecules are light enough to float away
There are no forces at all between the molecules
Only weak forces hold the molecules together
mcqs.explain: Substances made of small molecules have only weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

mcqs.q: When liquid water boils, what is overcome?
options: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
The intermolecular forces between the water molecules
Both the covalent bonds and the forces between them
The molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen
mcqs.explain: It is the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a substance boils.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a substance made of small molecules is correct?
options: Covalent bonds are the weakest forces in the substance
Intermolecular forces act inside each molecule
Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds
There are no forces at all between the molecules
mcqs.explain: The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak compared with the covalent bonds inside them.

mcqs.q: Methane, CH4, boils at -162 degrees C while octane, C8H18, boils at 126 degrees C. Why is octane's boiling point so much higher?
options: Octane molecules are heavier, so they need more heat energy
Octane has more covalent bonds that must be broken first
Octane is a liquid, and liquids always boil high
Its molecules are larger, so the forces are stronger
mcqs.explain: Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.

mcqs.q: Why does liquid octane not conduct electricity?
options: Its molecules have no overall electric charge
It has no metal atoms to carry the charge along
Liquids are not able to conduct electricity at all
Its electrons are locked inside the atoms themselves
mcqs.explain: Conduction needs charged particles free to move, and molecules are neutral overall.

mcqs.q: The bonds inside a Cl2 molecule are strong, yet chlorine boils at -34 degrees C. Which statement explains this?
options: The strong covalent bonds break as the chlorine boils
Some covalent bonds break and some are left whole
Boiling only has to overcome weak forces between molecules
Chlorine molecules have nothing holding them close
mcqs.explain: The strong covalent bonds are not broken; only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

mcqs.q: Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature?
options: Covalent bonds join each polymer chain to the next one
It is a giant covalent structure just like diamond
Its molecules are far too heavy to move at all
Its very large molecules attract each other strongly
mcqs.explain: Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong.

mcqs.q: A diagram shows a long chain of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with the chain continuing at both ends. What does it show?
options: A polymer built from large molecules
A giant covalent structure such as silica
A metal, since the atoms lie in a line
A small molecule such as ethene gas
mcqs.explain: Continuation marks and a repeating covalently bonded chain identify a polymer molecule.

mcqs.q: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?
options: Its intermolecular forces are very strong
Strong covalent bonds must be overcome
Strong forces hold its oppositely charged ions
Its atoms are heavy and hard to pull apart
mcqs.explain: All the atoms in a giant covalent structure are linked by strong covalent bonds, which must be overcome to melt it.

mcqs.q: A diagram shows every carbon atom bonded to four other carbon atoms in a continuous network. What does the diagram show?
options: A very large molecule of carbon, like C60
A giant metallic lattice of carbon atoms
A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A giant covalent structure, such as diamond
mcqs.explain: Every atom linked to other atoms by covalent bonds throughout the structure identifies a giant covalent structure.

mcqs.q: Why do most metals have high melting points and boiling points?
options: The metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong
The atoms in a metal are heavy and packed very tightly
Metals are hard, and hard materials melt slowly
Delocalised electrons stop the atoms escaping
mcqs.explain: Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding, so most have high melting and boiling points.

mcqs.q: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?
options: The two metals react to make a new compound entirely
Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding
The alloy contains far more delocalised electrons
The added atoms are heavier and much harder
mcqs.explain: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers that can slide; different sized atoms disrupt those layers.

mcqs.q: Why are metals good conductors of electricity and of thermal energy?
options: The metal ions are free to move around the metal
The atoms are packed so tightly that energy passes
Delocalised electrons carry charge and energy
Protons in the metal carry the electric charge along
mcqs.explain: The delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal and also transfer thermal energy.
